issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette: Rajesh, a 64-year-old married South Asian man, had worked in a warehouse for over two decades. His life took a drastic turn when he was taken captive by a group of armed men during a delivery to a remote area. For hours, Rajesh was held at gunpoint, unable to escape or call for help. The traumatic event left an indelible mark on his mind and behavior. Rajesh's memories of the event still lingered vividly, especially around the same time of day it occurred. He would become restless and anxious, feeling an overwhelming urge to be constantly on the move. His wife noticed that he would often glance at his watch, his eyes widening as the clock struck the fateful hour. These triggers also led Rajesh to develop a phobia of snakes, stemming from the snake-infested area where he was held captive. Merely hearing someone talk about snakes or seeing their photos would send shivers down his spine. Nighttime and darkness also terrified him; the blackness seemed to amplify every creak and groan in the warehouse, making him feel like an easy target. To cope with these triggers, Rajesh developed a range of maladaptive strategies. He began avoiding sleep or lying in the dark, often staying awake for hours, watching TV or browsing his phone to distract himself from the memories that haunted him. He would frequently ask his wife and colleagues to reassure him that he was okay, seeking constant validation to calm his frayed nerves. Rajesh also became obsessed with monitoring his body for signs of danger or injury, constantly checking for any unusual sensations or marks. As a result of these triggers and maladaptive strategies, Rajesh's sense of threat escalated. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, often staying vigilant, listening intently for any sounds that might indicate someone was lurking nearby. His hypervigilance extended beyond nighttime; he would frequently look behind him to check if someone was following him, even in familiar environments like his own neighborhood. Rajesh's experiences and strategies had also shaped his negative appraisals of himself and the world around him. He felt helpless, unable to stop bad things from happening to him, a sentiment that echoed through every aspect of his life. He began questioning whether his life was worth living anymore, feeling like he was just going through the motions without any purpose or joy. The thought of thinking about the event itself terrified Rajesh; he believed that confronting those memories would push him over the edge. As time passed, these negative appraisals fueled Rajesh's sense of threat even further. His conviction that he couldn't stop bad things from happening made him more alert and watchful, perpetuating a cycle of hypervigilance. Moreover, his maladaptive strategies reinforced his negative appraisals; the more he sought reassurance or monitored his body for signs of danger, the more he felt like he was losing control. In recent months, Rajesh's avoidance behaviors had taken a toll on his daily life and relationships. His wife grew tired of his constant requests for reassurance, feeling like she couldn't provide enough comfort to ease his fears. At work, Rajesh struggled to focus, his mind constantly drifting back to the traumatic event. He began calling in sick more frequently, unable to face the warehouse environment that reminded him of his captivity. What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a severe panic attack he experienced during a nighttime delivery. As he lay awake in bed afterward, he realized that he couldn't continue living like this – trapped by his memories and fears. He longed for a sense of peace and normalcy, hoping that therapy could help him break free from the cycle of threat and avoidance that had consumed his life.
